lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can a tick bite really make you allergic to meat?
It can. Imagine eating a burger for dinner, feeling completely fine, and then waking up in the middle of the night covered in hives, your throat swelling. Hours after the meal.
It's called alpha-gal syndrome. The US Centers for Disease Control estimates that up to 450,000 Americans may have been affected since 2010. And it's spreading.
lines.say: It's called alpha-gal syndrome. The US Centers for Disease Control estimates that up to four hundred and fifty thousand Americans may have been affected since twenty ten. And it's spreading.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: And it all starts with a tick?
In the United States, mostly with one tick in particular, the lone star tick. So let's see how one tiny bite can rewire your immune system.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: What exactly is alpha-gal?
It's a sugar molecule. Not the kind in sweets, but a tiny sugar tag stuck on the outside of cells. Cows, pigs, sheep, deer, cats and dogs, almost all mammals have it.
But you don't. Humans, apes and Old World monkeys lost the working gene to make it, millions of years ago.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Why would we lose it?

Nobody knows for sure. One idea is that it helped our ancestors fight germs. Many microbes carry alpha-gal tags, and since our own cells don't, our immune system can attack anything that does. In fact, all of us carry antibodies against it.
Normally, those antibodies are harmless. The trouble starts when the immune system makes the allergic kind.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So where does the tick come in?

Meet the lone star tick. The adult female has a single white spot on her back, which gives the tick its name. It's common across the southern and eastern United States, and it actively hunts for people and pets.
It doesn't spread Lyme disease, but it can carry other infections. And its bite can leave something much stranger behind.
When it bites, it pumps saliva into your skin. Researchers think that saliva carries alpha-gal, or something very much like it, along with chemicals that put your immune system on high alert.
In some people, the immune system responds by making IgE, the antibody behind allergies. From then on, alpha-gal looks like an enemy.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Does every tick bite do this?
No. Most bites don't, and scientists still don't know why some people develop it and others don't. Other ticks have been linked to it too.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Why does the reaction take hours?
That's what makes it so strange. Most food allergies hit within minutes. Alpha-gal reactions usually start two to six hours after eating.
In one study, patients ate pork or beef sausage under a doctor's watch. Not one of them reacted in the first two and a half hours. On average, the reaction came after about four.
The leading idea is that much of the alpha-gal in meat is attached to fat. Fat is digested slowly, packed into tiny fat particles, and only reaches your blood hours after the meal.
So the reaction often strikes in the middle of the night, long after dinner. That's why so many people never connect it to the burger.
Symptoms range from hives and itching to stomach pain, vomiting and swelling. In the worst cases, it's anaphylaxis, a whole-body reaction that can be deadly.

lines.speaker: q
lines.ch: A cancer drug cracked the case
lines.text: How did anyone figure this out?

Through a mystery in cancer clinics. In the mid-2000s, doctors in North Carolina noticed that a new cancer drug called cetuximab was causing severe allergic reactions far more often there than in other places.
lines.say: Through a mystery in cancer clinics. In the mid two thousands, doctors in North Carolina noticed that a new cancer drug called cetuximab was causing severe allergic reactions far more often there than in other places.

lines.text: In 2008, researchers found out why. The drug was made partly in mouse cells, so it carried alpha-gal. And the patients who reacted already had allergic antibodies against it, before their very first dose.
lines.say: In two thousand and eight, researchers found out why. The drug was made partly in mouse cells, so it carried alpha-gal. And the patients who reacted already had allergic antibodies against it, before their very first dose.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: But where did those antibodies come from?

That was the puzzle. Allergists, including Thomas Platts-Mills at the University of Virginia, noticed the same antibodies in people with delayed reactions to red meat. And the cases clustered where the lone star tick lives.
By 2011, they had linked the antibodies to tick bites. An allergy that hides for hours, and starts with a bite. Nobody had seen anything like it.
lines.say: By twenty eleven, they had linked the antibodies to tick bites. An allergy that hides for hours, and starts with a bite. Nobody had seen anything like it.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Is it only red meat?
Red meat is the main problem: beef, pork, lamb, venison and rabbit. Chicken, turkey and fish are fine, because birds and fish don't make alpha-gal.
But some people also react to milk and cheese, or to gelatin, which is made from animal collagen. Gelatin hides in sweets, marshmallows, and even in some medicine capsules.
A few very sensitive people have even reacted to the fumes from cooking meat, just walking past a barbecue.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So turkey at Christmas is still safe?
The turkey itself, yes. Just check the gravy if it's made with beef stock, and the gelatin in some desserts.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Why are we hearing about it so much more?
Because the lone star tick is on the move. Once mostly a southern tick, it's now found across much of the Midwest and the Northeast, as far north as New York and Maine.
Scientists point to milder winters, more deer and wild turkeys for the ticks to feed on, and suburbs spreading into woodland.
In Arkansas, the first state to require labs to report suspected cases, the number more than doubled in the first half of 2026, compared with the same months a year earlier.
lines.say: In Arkansas, the first state to require labs to report suspected cases, the number more than doubled in the first half of twenty twenty-six, compared with the same months a year earlier.

lines.text: And many doctors still miss it. In a 2022 CDC survey of fifteen hundred US health care providers, forty-two percent had never even heard of alpha-gal syndrome.
lines.say: And many doctors still miss it. In a twenty twenty-two CDC survey of fifteen hundred US health care providers, forty-two percent had never even heard of alpha-gal syndrome.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can it actually kill you?
Rarely, but yes. In 2024, a healthy 47-year-old man in New Jersey ate a hamburger at a barbecue. About four hours later he fell ill, and he died.
lines.say: Rarely, but yes. In twenty twenty-four, a healthy forty-seven-year-old man in New Jersey ate a hamburger at a barbecue. About four hours later he fell ill, and he died.

lines.text: Two weeks earlier, he'd had a frightening reaction a few hours after eating steak on a camping trip. Nobody had linked it to meat.

The autopsy found no clear cause. But when researchers tested his blood afterwards, they found alpha-gal antibodies, and a marker of severe allergic reaction far higher than they'd ever seen. In 2025, they reported it as the first known death from alpha-gal syndrome.
lines.say: The autopsy found no clear cause. But when researchers tested his blood afterwards, they found alpha-gal antibodies, and a marker of severe allergic reaction far higher than they'd ever seen. In twenty twenty-five, they reported it as the first known death from alpha-gal syndrome.

lines.text: His wife remembered a dozen or so tiny bites around his ankles that summer. The researchers think they were bites from lone star tick larvae, which many people mistake for chiggers.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Is there a cure?
Not yet. The main treatment is avoiding mammal meat and other alpha-gal products, and carrying emergency medicine if a doctor prescribes it.
Medicines need checking too. A 2022 review found that many commonly prescribed drugs contain animal-derived ingredients that may carry alpha-gal, although alternatives are usually available.
lines.say: Medicines need checking too. A twenty twenty-two review found that many commonly prescribed drugs contain animal-derived ingredients that may carry alpha-gal, although alternatives are usually available.

lines.text: There is some good news. For some people, the allergy fades over months or years, as long as they don't get bitten again. But a new bite can bring it right back.
Because the reaction comes so late, many patients keep a food diary, writing down every meal and the time any symptoms appear, to spot the pattern.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: I've heard it's linked to heart disease too?

That's still being studied. In 2018, researchers at the University of Virginia linked alpha-gal antibodies to more fatty plaque in the arteries of the heart, and a larger study in 2022 pointed the same way. It doesn't prove that the antibodies cause heart disease.
lines.say: That's still being studied. In twenty eighteen, researchers at the University of Virginia linked alpha-gal antibodies to more fatty plaque in the arteries of the heart, and a larger study in twenty twenty-two pointed the same way. It doesn't prove that the antibodies cause heart disease.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How do I avoid it?
Avoid the bite. Walk in the middle of trails, cover your skin, and treat your clothes and gear with permethrin.
Permethrin goes on fabric, not on skin. For your skin, health agencies recommend a registered insect repellent, such as one with DEET or picaridin.
lines.say: Permethrin goes on fabric, not on skin. For your skin, health agencies recommend a registered insect repellent, such as one with deet or picaridin.

lines.text: After being outdoors, check yourself, your kids and your pets. If you find a tick attached, grab it close to the skin with fine-tipped tweezers and pull it straight out.
Skip the old tricks. Don't burn it, and don't smother it in nail polish or petroleum jelly. Just pull it out, and clean the bite.
And if you ever wake up with hives hours after a steak, tell your doctor about any tick bites. A simple blood test can check for alpha-gal antibodies.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So one bite can really change what I can eat?
It can. A sugar your body never made, a tick that slips it under your skin, and an immune system that never forgets. It's one of the strangest allergies ever found.
A tick bite can make you allergic to meat.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Subscribe for more of the weird ways your body works, and tell us in the comments if you'd ever heard of alpha-gal before today.
